message: [PULSE-16] Bronze design question while I am in 002_bronze_tables.sql - every column lands as text, including things that are obviously integers. Any objections?
[PULSE-16] None. A cast at the bronze boundary is a silent filter - anything that will not cast becomes a null or an exception and the original is gone either way.

[PULSE-18] Honest admission for ADR-001: my instinct was to filter bad rows at load. It felt tidy. Geetha talked me out of it and I would like the rejected version recorded rather than quietly overwritten.
[PULSE-18] Recorded as the rejected alternative. An ADR that only records the winning argument is half an ADR.

PR #14 up for PULSE-14 - generator schemas for customers, products, orders and lines. About 400 lines but most of it is the reference tables. Would like a look at the seeding, since everything downstream depends on it being reproducible.

Reviewed PULSE-14. One change requested: the seed is read once at module import, so two generator calls in the same process share a stream and the second one is not reproducible on its own. Pass the seed into the constructor instead.
Good catch, fixed and pushed. PULSE-14 now takes the seed per call and I added a test that generates twice in one process and asserts the frames are identical.

PULSE-17 detail worth flagging: a missing source file is an error, but a present file with zero rows is a warning with the count recorded. A silent zero-row extract looks exactly like a quiet business day until someone asks why last Tuesday is missing.
[PULSE-14] Ran the largest generator preset overnight - 4.2m order lines in about nine minutes, deterministic across two machines with the same seed. That is good enough to load test against.

[PULSE-15] Seeding the deliberate defects into the generator now: replayed orders, negative quantities, loyalty tier case drift, 0.07% of customers with no email, a few orphan customer ids, weekend FX gaps. Each at a documented rate so a test can assert both that we caught them and how many there should be.
[PULSE-15] That last part is what makes the quality epic testable rather than aspirational.

Reviewing PULSE-16. The bronze DDL is fine, but every table repeats the same five metadata columns by hand. If we add a sixth we will miss one - worth a small generator or at least a comment block that says these five must stay in step.
Fair. Pulled them into a template applied per table in PULSE-16, so the metadata columns are declared once.

PR up for PULSE-20, the bronze loader. The idempotency is per run_id: a re-run deletes its own rows and reloads, so a partial load cannot leave half a file behind. Worth a careful read of the delete predicate.
Read it twice. The predicate is scoped to run_id and source file, which is right - scoping to run_id alone would have wiped the other seven sources on a single-file retry. Approving PULSE-20.
[PULSE-23] Something is off. Order line count does not match the header count and the gap is suspiciously stable at about 1.2%. Digging.
[PULSE-23] Found it - every missing order id starts with a zero. 0004821 is landing in bronze as 4821.

[PULSE-23] That is the CSV reader inferring dtypes. Which is exactly the failure ADR-001 predicted, three days after we wrote ADR-001. Nothing errored, nothing was logged, the rows just quietly stopped matching.

[PULSE-23] Raising this to High. Silent data loss is top of the list of things I do not want in this platform. Please also add a check that asserts header to line join completeness, so this class of thing cannot come back unnoticed.
[PULSE-23] Fixed with an explicit dtype map. The join completeness assertion goes into the reconciliation set in PULSE-40.

Small review note on PULSE-21: the backoff is retrying on 4xx as well as 5xx. A 401 is not going to fix itself in eight seconds, and six retries against a bad credential is a good way to get the key blocked.
Correct, that is sloppy. Retrying 429 and 5xx only, everything else fails immediately with the status and endpoint in the message. Pushed to PULSE-21.

PULSE-23 fix is up. The diff is small - an explicit dtype map in the reader - but I have added the header-to-line count assertion to the same PR so the fix and the thing that would have caught it land together.

[PULSE-31] Pipeline skeleton is six stages run in sequence. Explicitly not adding an orchestrator - six stages and one schedule do not need Dagster. I am keeping the stage boundaries clean so it becomes a wrapper when we do need it, and I will raise the ticket now with the trigger condition written down.
[PULSE-28] About 0.9% of orders arrive more than once - the source replays on retry. Collapsing on order_id with a window over ingest time.

[PULSE-29] Careful with the survivor rule there. Ingest order and business order are not the same thing, and the difference is the status field. If an order was replayed as pending then completed, keeping the first row loses the revenue.
You are right and it is doing exactly that. About 0.3% of completed orders silently excluded. Raised as PULSE-29.
Second silent bug in three weeks, and both were caught by comparing counts across layers rather than by anything failing. That feels like it should shape the quality epic.

Agreed, and it does - the reconciliation checks in PULSE-40 are precisely that idea made systematic. Everything else verifies that data looks reasonable. Reconciliations verify that two things we computed separately agree.

PULSE-28 is up. The de-dupe is a ROW_NUMBER over order_id ordered by updated_at desc, ingested_at desc. Please look hard at the ordering - it is the whole correctness of the story and I have already had it wrong once.

Ordering is right now. One more thing for PULSE-28: the dedupe count needs to go into the run context, otherwise a sudden jump in replays is invisible. Right now we would only find out by noticing revenue moved.

CI on PULSE-31 went red on the Postgres job and green on DuckDB. It is a cast - Postgres will not implicitly compare a text column to an integer literal. Not a flake, a real difference, which is the argument for running both.
That is the second time this week. Adding a note to the SQL style section of the README: cast explicitly at the silver boundary, never rely on the engine to guess. Ticketed under PULSE-31.

[PULSE-35] Starting gold.analysis_window. It is one table and about eleven lines of SQL and I think it will end up being the highest-leverage thing in the warehouse. Every recency metric anchors to MAX(order_date), not to the clock, so a screenshot from April still matches the warehouse in September.
[PULSE-35] The test that greps the analytics SQL for CURRENT_DATE is what makes it stick. A convention without an assertion is a suggestion, and someone will write CURRENT_DATE at 6pm on a Friday.
[PULSE-35] Merged with the test. It already caught one usage in a draft mart I had open.

[PULSE-34] FX decision: convert at the rate on the order date, not today's rate. Restating history every time the currency moves makes last month's report disagree with itself and no explanation of that is ever satisfying.
[PULSE-34] Carry-forward fills are flagged in a column so a check can count them. About 28% of dates are carried, which is just what weekends are.
PULSE-35 is a tiny PR - one view and a test - but it touches every recency metric we will ever write, so I would rather two reviews than one. Deven, Divya, when you get a moment.
Approved PULSE-35. The grep test is doing more work than the view is. One suggestion: have it fail with the offending file and line rather than just a count, so the fix is obvious from the CI log.

[PULSE-37] Check framework design note: every check carries a plain-language description of what a failure means in business terms. A check called chk_cust_email_not_null tells whoever reads the alert nothing about whether to care.

[PULSE-38] And the results table appends rather than overwrites. A check that has been drifting for three weeks is a different problem from one that broke last night, and you cannot tell them apart from a snapshot.

Review note on PULSE-37: the check API takes a threshold as a bare float, so 0.15 could be a fraction or a percentage depending on who wrote the check. Two of the twenty-four already disagree. Make it explicit in the parameter name or take a typed threshold.
Both of those were mine. Renamed to threshold_pct throughout PULSE-37 and fixed the two that were wrong. That would have been an interesting bug to find at 3am.

That history is also the foundation drift detection will need eventually. Raising PULSE-121 now, while we are building the table, because it would be irritating to want it in six months with nothing to compare against.
[PULSE-43] Test fixture is session-scoped. Function scope was correct and took four minutes, which meant nobody would ever run it locally, which makes it worse than incorrect.
[PULSE-40] Rounding tolerance on the line-to-header reconciliation is 0.01 per order, absolute rather than relative. A relative tolerance on a small order is meaningless.

PULSE-39 PR has all 24 checks. It is a big diff but it is 24 near-identical declarations, so read the first three carefully and skim the rest - or tell me the declaration shape is wrong and I will redo them all now rather than at check number sixty.
Shape is right. Approving PULSE-39. The plain-language failure description on each one is what will make these readable in six months.
PULSE-43: got the fixture from four minutes to 26 seconds by moving to session scope and dropping the largest preset from the default run. The big dataset is behind a marker for the nightly job.

PULSE-46 is up - all seven dimensions. Reviewing your own conformed dimensions is hard, so what I actually want checked is whether the customer dimension can be joined by orders, payments and events without any of them needing a special case.
Checked all three join paths on PULSE-46, no special cases. Events needed the natural key trimmed before matching, which I have pushed into silver rather than into the join.

Conformed is the word doing the work in PULSE-46. One customer dimension, joined by orders, payments and events alike. The moment there are two, 'customers who bought' and 'customers who clicked' become unjoinable and nobody notices until the funnel numbers disagree.

[PULSE-47] The check counting fact rows on surrogate key -1 is the whole point of the Unknown member. An Unknown member without a count is the same silent data loss as an inner join, just with better manners.
[PULSE-47] 0.31% of order facts land on customer -1, which matches the seeded orphan ids exactly. Good - the number is real and we know what it is.
[PULSE-49] Genuine question rather than a challenge: two facts holding the same revenue looks like duplication to me. What stops them drifting apart?

[PULSE-50] Reconciliation check one, which fails the build if they disagree by more than a penny per order. And the duplication is the point - one line-grain fact plus a distinct-count discipline means the discipline lives in the head of whoever writes the query. Two explicit facts make the AOV mistake structurally impossible rather than discouraged in review.
[PULSE-50] That is a good answer and I would like it in the ADR, including my objection. It is the obvious challenge and the ADR should answer it rather than pretend nobody raised it.

PULSE-49 review: fact_sales rebuilds by truncate and insert inside a transaction, which is fine, but the transaction wraps the whole build and holds a lock for about ninety seconds on the largest preset. Worth knowing before this meets a live dashboard.
Noted on PULSE-49. Leaving it for now since nothing reads the warehouse during a build, but I have put it in the ticket so it is not a surprise when something does.
[PULSE-54] Is building a Type 2 customer dimension with exactly one version per customer worth doing right now?

[PULSE-54] Fair challenge. It is worth it because every downstream consumer writes its joins against the shape, and retrofitting valid_from into thirty existing queries is the expensive version. But the file header says plainly that the shape is real and the history is not, so nobody builds a tier-at-time-of-purchase analysis on it and gets a confidently wrong answer. Real change capture is PULSE-119.
[PULSE-56] AOV in the draft sales mart is about 40% below what finance calculates by hand. Checking.
[PULSE-56] It is the grain. I computed AVG(net_amount) over fact_sales, which is line grain. That is the average line value, not the average order value. Exactly the thing we wrote down in March.

[PULSE-56] We documented the trap in March and walked into it in June. I am not treating that as a documentation failure though - the document is how you knew to be suspicious of the number. But documentation does not run nightly, so it needs an assertion behind it.
[PULSE-56] Adding my vote for the check. Two explicit facts made the mistake possible to detect. Only an assertion makes it impossible to ship.
[PULSE-56] Fixed and the check is in. Retro item: any metric with a grain judgement in its definition gets an assertion when it is first implemented, not when it first goes wrong.
PULSE-53 before and after, sales by region by month on the largest preset: 8.4s to 0.6s. The date key index is nearly all of it. EXPLAIN is in the ticket for both engines.
PULSE-56 hotfix is up - AOV moves to fact_orders and there is a check asserting the mart figure against a header-grain recomputation. Deliberately kept the check in the same PR as the fix.
Approved PULSE-56. Same-PR is right. A fix without the assertion is a fix that comes back.

[PULSE-58] theme.py before the first chart, not after the thirtieth. One palette, one hue per entity across every page, fixed categorical order, sequential ramps for magnitude only, and no dual axes ever. Retrofitting consistency across a built estate costs an order of magnitude more and half of it never gets done.

[PULSE-58] Fixed categorical order has already earned itself. A bar chart sorted by value redrew in a different order between two refreshes and I misread the change as a data problem for about ten minutes.
PULSE-57 review request. The rule I am trying to hold is that no page issues SQL - everything goes through data_access. If you see a query anywhere in pages/, that is the bug.
One found in PULSE-57, on the executive page. Also the cache TTL is hardcoded in three places with two different values, which will be confusing at exactly the wrong moment.

[PULSE-63] Framing I want to check with you both: the quality suite asserts things about the data on every run, the test suite asserts things about the code on every push. Both matter, they are not substitutes, and that distinction was not obvious to me from the outside.
[PULSE-63] That is clearer than how we have been describing it internally. Worth putting in the README, not just the strategy doc.

[PULSE-62] Read through the KPI document and the four ADRs. The thing that stands out is that most of your past bugs were silent rather than loud - wrong numbers rather than crashes. So my gap analysis is going to be mostly about assertions between layers rather than more unit tests.
PULSE-58 is up. theme.py is small on purpose - a palette, a category order, and three chart helpers. If a page needs a colour that is not in here, that is a conversation rather than a local override.

[PULSE-62] Gap analysis done. Three areas with no coverage at all: the dashboards, the analytics modules, and anything asserting that the ops tables survive a full warehouse rebuild. The third one worries me most, because a rebuild is routine and the streaming layer will land in those tables.
That third one is a good instinct and it is now PULSE-86. Welcome aboard - that is a better first-week output than I asked for.
PULSE-65 sales page is up for review. Four filters, and they compose, which is where I would expect bugs. Worth trying combinations that return nothing.
Went through PULSE-65 filter combinations. Empty result renders a blank chart with no explanation - looks like a loading state. Everything else held up.
[PULSE-69] Executive page went from 1.1s to 4.6s on the largest preset after the region filter landed. Not visible at all on the demo data, which is why it is worth testing against something bigger.

[PULSE-69] Filter was applied in Python after loading the full result set, and the cache key did not include the filter values so every change was a cache miss on a full scan. Pushed into SQL, back to 0.9s.

Raising PULSE-66 - the revenue and margin chart on the sales page uses a secondary y-axis, and ADR-004 says never. Raising it from the written rule rather than from taste, which is much easier to have a conversation about.
[PULSE-66] Guilty. It was the quickest way to get both series in one place and I talked myself into it. Splitting into two aligned charts.

[PULSE-66] This is the ADR earning its keep in a code review, which is exactly what it is for. The series cross in September in the demo data and that crossing point is pure artefact of the two scales.
PULSE-69 fix is up. Two lines: the filter moves into the SQL and the filter values go into the cache key. The second one is the actual bug - the cache was returning a hit for a different filter set.
That is worse than the slowness then - PULSE-69 could have shown one region's numbers under another region's filter. Did it?

No - the key was missing the filter but the query was unfiltered too, so it was returning the full set and filtering after. Slow, not wrong. But you are right that it was one line away from being wrong, and silently. Adding a cache key test to PULSE-69.
[PULSE-71] Zero-order customers stay in customer_360. They are the denominator of activation, and filtering them out here is exactly how an activation problem becomes invisible.

[PULSE-75] Churn in a non-contractual business is a judgement, not an observation - nobody cancels, they just stop. Writing the window rule down with its arbitrariness admitted rather than presenting it as measured fact.

[PULSE-76] CLV uses an explainable formula rather than a fitted probabilistic model. Marketing has to defend an acquisition budget with this number, and a number they cannot explain is a number they cannot defend.

PULSE-72 up for review. The RFM quintiles use NTILE over the active base, and the segment naming is a CASE ladder. The ladder is ugly but it is readable and it matches the boundaries in the KPI doc line for line, which I care about more.
Approving PULSE-72. Agreed on the ladder - a clever version that does not visibly match the document is worse.
[PULSE-74] The cohort chart has a 60% cliff between period 0 and period 1 and I cannot explain it. Something is wrong with the definition rather than the data.

[PULSE-74] Got it. Cohorts are built on signup month, and a large share of signups never purchase at all. They enter a cohort and leave without ever having been a customer. The cliff is the activation rate wearing a retention costume - and it was three days from being presented to the board as a retention crisis.

[PULSE-74] Second time a definition choice has produced a plausible and completely misleading picture. AOV was the first. Both caught by someone thinking a number looked odd, not by anything automated.

[PULSE-74] And I do not think that is fully fixable with assertions. A definition can be internally consistent and still answer the wrong question. What we can do is require every cohort-shaped metric to state its membership rule on the chart itself, so a reader can catch what a test cannot.

[PULSE-74] I can assert the mechanical half: cohort size must equal the count of customers whose first order is in that month. It will not catch a bad definition but it will catch a regression away from the good one.

[PULSE-74] Both done. And the activation finding goes to the business as a finding rather than being quietly absorbed into a definition change - it is genuinely the more useful of the two discoveries.

[PULSE-77] Determinism assertion is in the customer pack - two runs on the same data must produce byte-identical output. It is the property that makes every other test meaningful and it is invisible until it breaks.
PULSE-73 rewritten on first purchase month. Diff is bigger than it looks because the cohort key changes shape - please check the period number arithmetic rather than the join.

[PULSE-7] Streaming design, two rules. One: event time, never wall-clock time, or we can never replay a stream and get the same KPIs back. Two: the consumer owns no metric definitions - it lands events and recomputes a window, and every metric stays in SQL next to the batch ones.

[PULSE-7] Seconding rule two hard. Revenue must not mean two different things depending on which pipeline produced it. That is the failure mode that ends with two dashboards disagreeing in a board meeting.
[PULSE-83] Rule one is just ADR-002 applied to streaming. Same principle, same reason: anchor to the data, not to the clock.

[PULSE-79] Bus abstraction with a file implementation and a Kafka implementation. Without the file version, CI needs a broker, every test becomes slow and flaky, and streaming ends up as the untested corner of the platform.
[PULSE-79] That is the difference between me being able to test this path and not. Running the consumer against files in CI is the same code path as against Redpanda.
PULSE-79 bus interface is up. Three methods and two implementations. If the abstraction is wrong this is the cheapest moment to say so - once the consumer is written against it, it is not.
Reviewed PULSE-79. commit() taking the whole batch rather than an offset is the right call - it keeps the offset bookkeeping inside the bus instead of in every consumer.

[PULSE-82] At-least-once with idempotent writes keyed on event id, rather than chasing exactly-once. Exactly-once here would mean a distributed transaction across the broker and the warehouse, for a KPI window that recomputes anyway.

[PULSE-82] Crash test written - kill the consumer mid-batch, restart, assert no duplicates and no gaps. It passes now, and it failed against an earlier build where the commit came before the write, so the test is doing real work rather than confirming what we already believed.
PULSE-82 consumer is up. The bit to review hardest is the ordering: write, commit transaction, then commit offset. Any other order loses events or duplicates them, and both failure modes are quiet.

Reviewed PULSE-82 by trying to break it rather than by reading it. Killed the process between the transaction commit and the offset commit - it reprocesses the batch on restart and the idempotent write absorbs it. That is the behaviour we want.

[PULSE-87] The staleness indicator on the real-time page is the important part of it. A live dashboard silently showing a fifteen-minute-old number is worse than one that says the feed is down, because people act on it.
[PULSE-87] Tested by stopping the producer. It flags stale after the threshold and stops presenting the window as current.

PULSE-85 fix is up. Three parts: ops DDL moves to its own file, everything becomes CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, and the pipeline no longer runs the ops DDL at all - it is init-only. Neha's test goes red on main and green on the branch.
Approved PULSE-85. The part I would not have thought of is making it init-only rather than just non-destructive. A pipeline that cannot touch ops at all is a much smaller thing to reason about.
PULSE-88 is deliberately boring - it reads ops.realtime_kpis and returns it. If anyone is tempted to add a computed field here, that is the moment we have two definitions of a metric again.

[PULSE-91] Attribution approach: we are not picking a model. Five models, side by side, one row per channel and one column per model. No model here is correct, and publishing one would be a confident answer to a question we cannot answer - which would then immediately become 'the number'.

[PULSE-90] Related discipline: the attribution basis goes in the column name. revenue_last_touch, not revenue. A column called revenue in a marketing mart is a lie by omission, because it is always attributed somehow.

[PULSE-90] Unattributed revenue gets its own line rather than being distributed proportionally. It is 34% of the total. Spreading it would have hidden the single most important caveat about this whole mart.

PULSE-91 is up. Five attribution models over the same event set. The models share a touchpoint builder and differ only in the credit function, which keeps the diff between them honest - if they disagree it is the model, not the plumbing.
Reviewed PULSE-91. Suggest asserting that the five models each sum to the same total attributed revenue. If one of them does not, the credit function is leaking and the comparison is meaningless.
Added to PULSE-91, and time decay was out by 0.4% from a rounding accumulation. Would have been very hard to spot on a chart.
[PULSE-91] The spread is the finding. One influencer channel comes out at 1.8x ROAS on last touch and 6.1x on first touch, and it has had its budget cut for two quarters on the last-touch number.

[PULSE-91] Walked through the attribution work this morning. From the business side the useful reframing might be: the question is not which model is right, it is which channels the models disagree about - because those are the ones where the budget decision is actually a bet rather than a calculation.
[PULSE-91] That is a better articulation than mine and it is going on the dashboard.

[PULSE-94] On labelling the incrementality proxy - put it next to the number rather than in a tooltip or a footnote. In my experience the footnote does not survive the screenshot, and the screenshot is what reaches the decision.

[PULSE-97] Traceability draft covers 34 of 41 requirements. The empty cells are the useful part - three requirements have a dashboard tile and no test, and one has a test and no definition, which is the more interesting way round.
[PULSE-106] The three with a tile and no test are going into the analytics regression pack this sprint.
[PULSE-98] First forecast run: Holt-Winters, MAPE 12.4%. Which reads as respectable until you have something to compare it against.

[PULSE-98] Backtested it against seasonal naive. The naive baseline wins on the daily series at 11.8%. Holt-Winters wins clearly on the weekly aggregate. So the honest answer is that it depends on the series, which is not the answer anyone wants.

[PULSE-99] Which is exactly why the baseline gets published as a first-class result, same table, same chart, same visual weight. Presenting Holt-Winters alone would have shipped a model that adds nothing at daily grain and nobody would have known.
[PULSE-99] Same visual weight deliberately. A baseline rendered as a faint dashed line is a baseline being argued against rather than reported.
[PULSE-101] Churn model scores 0.94 AUC. Raising a bug against my own work - 0.94 on a churn model built in an afternoon is not a good sign, it is a symptom.

[PULSE-101] Leakage, as suspected. Features were computed at the same moment as the label, so recency_days effectively was the label. A customer is labelled churned because they have not purchased recently, and I handed the model exactly that.
[PULSE-101] Correct instinct and worth saying plainly: a model that scores far better than the problem is hard is nearly always answering an easier question than the one you asked.

[PULSE-106] Adding a temporal validation assertion to the analytics pack - maximum feature timestamp must precede the label window start. Mechanical, but this class of bug is subtle to spot and trivial to assert.
[PULSE-100] Rebuilt with a 90-day rewind. 0.71 AUC, top decile carries about 3.4x the base churn rate, and it actually predicts. Neha's assertion is green.
PULSE-100 churn PR is up for review. The model is twenty lines; the feature snapshot is a hundred and fifty and that is where the bug was, so that is where the review time should go.

Reviewing PULSE-100 now. Coefficients need to come out in the scored output rather than only in the training log - the retention team cannot read our logs, and the whole argument for a linear model is that they can see why.

[PULSE-102] Writing ADR-005 while the numbers are fresh: logistic regression over the gradient-boosted model, which scored about 0.03 AUC better. The retention team has to know why a customer is at risk in order to write a campaign. A ranked list from a black box tells them who but not what to say.
[PULSE-102] With a revisit condition: when an action exists that needs only the ranking and not the reason. This is a decision about the current use case, not a permanent position on model families.
